When the parties 
to a written contract have agreed to it as an 
"integration"-a 
complete and final embodiment of the terms of an 
agreement- parol evidence cannot be used to add to or vary its terms. 
When only parL of the agreement is integrated, the same rule applies to 
that part, but parol evidence may be used to prove elements of the 
agreement not reduced to writing. 
The en. ·ial issue in determining 
whether there has 
been an 
integration IR whether the parties intended their writing to serve as the 
exclusive embodiment of their agreement. The instrument itself may 
help to resolw that issue. It may state, for example, that "there are no 
previous urn:lerstandings or agreements not contained in the writing,"

the parties' 
"intention 
to nullify

understandings or agreements." (See 3 Corbin, Contracts (1960) § 578, p. 
411.) Any such collateral agreement itself must be examined, however, 
to determine whether the parties intended the subjects of negotiation it 
deals with to be included in excluded from, or otherwise affected by the 
writing. Circumstances at the time of the writing may also aid in the 
determination of such integration ....
